title: Returning Results From Data Changes knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under 'Returning Results From Data Changes'?
options: A row value from a different unrelated table
questions.explanation: The source SQL syllabus lists 'Returning inserted records' as a subtopic of 'Returning Results From Data Changes'; this lesson connects that point to a PostgreSQL-oriented example.

questions.prompt: Which practice best supports reliable work with returning results from data changes?
options: Skip edge-case checks because the sample returns rows.
Preview target rows and constrain changes; use a transaction when several changes must succeed together.
Add unrelated clauses until the output looks plausible.
Assume the database engines behave identically.
questions.answer_key: Preview target rows and constrain changes; use a transaction when several changes must succeed together.
questions.explanation: Preview target rows and constrain changes; use a transaction when several changes must succeed together. The lesson keeps the distinction between core SQL concepts and engine-specific behavior explicit.

questions.prompt: When an example related to returning results from data changes produces an unexpected result, what should you do first?
options: Inspect a small result, test a boundary or missing-value case, and compare it with the documented behavior.
Run the same statement repeatedly without inspecting the data.
Remove constraints and access controls until the query succeeds.
Assume every SQL engine applies identical rules.
questions.answer_key: Inspect a small result, test a boundary or missing-value case, and compare it with the documented behavior.
questions.explanation: A small, controlled test makes query behavior explainable. Inspect the data shape, conditions, NULLs, ties, plan, or transaction state that applies to the specific topic.
